Additionally, when this upgrade package was added to others, we see a 2.1% increase in savings when comparing Upgrades 1 and 6, and a 1.1% increase in savings when comparing Upgrades 3 and 8. Of the building characteristics that PBC representatives were most interested in exploring in Task 1, we found that building age (vintage) had the greatest impact on the potential electricity savings of the various upgrades as compared to the baseline. Figure 12 shows that upgrades that include either ENERGY STAR Heat Pumps (Upgrades 1, 6, and 11) or Ultra-high Efficiency Heat Pumps (Upgrades 3, 8, and 13) generate more annual electricity savings for older households. Specifically, households built before 1960 have markedly higher modeled energy savings even compared to households built in the 1960s or 1970s. Additionally, we found that the difference between homes with different vintages was more pronounced for the upgrades that included Ultra-high Efficiency Heat Pumps (Upgrades 3, 8, and 13). While the energy savings potential of these older homes is larger, there may be other factors that may make these homes more costly to retrofit. These include lead paint, asbestos, and other legacy issues that may increase both the time and cost to retrofit a household. While not as significant, building type had an impact on annual electricity savings (Figure 13). In general, single-family detached and attached households experienced greater modeled annual electricity savings with heat pump upgrades as compared to mobile homes and multi-family households. However, this could be a function of the physical size of these buildings (i.e., single- family households have on average more conditioned space, both in terms of area and volume, and have more exterior facing walls). These larger households with larger building enclosure surface areas and more interior space to heat and cool will generally see greater amount of relative energy savings with the installation of increased efficiency HVAC systems. 13 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications.
